title: Parents' immigration and courtship; early work as streetcar driver
description: Ida Mae Cox, interviewed at age 95 in Lewiston by Cathy Naugle, recounts her father John Schmitt's birth in Germany in 1847 and his emigration to the United States as a stowaway at age 15. She describes his work as a merchant seaman and horse-drawn streetcar conductor in San Francisco and Spokane, and how his parents met through his military service around Omaha. The conversation covers her mother's birth in Iowa and their marriage in Omaha in 1875.

title: Homestead establishment; Indian ponies; baby brother's death in fire
description: The discussion moves to her parents' arrival in the Moscow area and their homestead, where her father acquired Indian ponies and captured wild horses. She details the construction of their first log cabin and a framed house, and recounts how her baby brother died from burns suffered in a house fire that also destroyed their first home, after which neighbors helped the family.

title: Mother's pregnancy loss; grave decoration; lack of physical affection in family
description: Ida Mae recounts visiting Uniontown and learning from her sister about their mother's miscarriage, which the mother never discussed. She recalls decorating her sister's grave with strawberries at age 16 or 17, and discusses how her parents never displayed physical affection toward their children, contrasting this with her own behavior toward her husband.

title: Migraine headaches; automobile accident and injuries
description: She describes suffering migraine headaches since childhood, hiding from others during severe attacks that lasted into her marriage. The conversation shifts to an automobile accident approximately 25 years prior that broke her shoulder and arm, the medical treatment she received, and her lengthy recovery.

title: Meeting husband Charlie; working for Henderson family; school attendance
description: Ida Mae describes working for the Henderson family at age 17, where she met her future husband Charlie, who worked on a threshing crew. She recounts her earlier courtship with George Whitney, who left for college, and discusses her limited schooling that ended after the fifth grade when she began working full time.

title: Marriage to Charlie; household furnishings; one daughter
description: She recalls marrying Charlie in Genesee at age 19 or 20 while he was 29, and describes their first home with minimal furnishings, including no plumbing initially. She explains she had only one daughter, contrasting with her mother's eight children, and describes the birth at home attended by a doctor and midwife.

title: Catering for 40 years; wedding cake baking
description: Ida Mae discusses her 40-year career as a cook and caterer, cooking and serving meals in homes for special occasions. She mentions baking a wedding cake for her sister-in-law in Yakima using pound cake with whipped cream filling, frozen at a creamery, and notes she never learned commercial cake decorating.

title: Hobbies and fair ribbons; rural life vs city life
description: Ida Mae discusses her hobbies, including skiing and entering baked goods and canned items in fairs. She then compares the busy lives of farm women to those of city women, noting that farm work involves caring for livestock and helping in the fields.

title: Working at the golf course; urban experiences
description: Ida Mae recounts the six years she and her husband spent building and caretaking a golf course in Lewiston. She reflects on how this period made her more of an urban woman, and mentions her attempts to play golf despite physical limitations.

title: Country living preferences; friendships and neighbors
description: She expresses her preference for rural living, where she can keep a cow and chickens. She then talks about her friends and neighbors, comparing their activity levels and describing visits to a lonely elderly neighbor.

title: Irene's education; parenting styles
description: Ida Mae discusses her determination to give her daughter a business college education, contrasting it with her own lack of schooling. She also reflects on how her parenting style differed from her mother's regarding physical affection.

title: Changing family sizes; birth control; marriage and sex
description: She discusses how the cost and purpose of raising children have changed over time. She shares her views on birth control, sexual relations, and the portrayal of sex on television.

title: The Great Depression; banking and financial independence
description: Ida Mae recalls the Great Depression and explains how keeping her money in a separate bank account allowed her to access funds when banks closed. She discusses the importance of financial independence for married women.

title: Health emergencies; retirement from work
description: She describes a severe nosebleed hemorrhage she suffered while catering a dinner party, which required emergency medical attention. This incident led to her retirement from catering, and she reflects on her need to keep busy.

title: World War II; views on marriage and women's liberation
description: Ida Mae shares her memories of the fear and blackouts during World War II, particularly after Pearl Harbor. She then discusses her belief in the institution of marriage and admits she knows little about the women's liberation movement.

title: Daughter's health crisis; advice and life reflections
description: She expresses worry about her daughter, who is undergoing kidney dialysis and recently had complications with her access port. She advises that adjusting to rural life depends on the individual and reflects on her own happy and unhappy times.

title: Dancing and social life; widowhood
description: Ida Mae fondly remembers her youth spent dancing until the early morning hours and traveling long distances by wagon. She explains why she never remarried after her husband's death and how she misses their companionship.
